hero.introParagraph: TeleDirectMD treats pediatric head lice (pediculosis capitis, ICD-10 B85.0) by secure video visit for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. A parent or legal guardian must be present and provide consent for every visit. Over-the-counter permethrin 1 percent remains first-line, and TeleDirectMD reserves prescription agents such as spinosad, ivermectin lotion, and benzyl alcohol for treatment failures or documented resistance. Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

telehealthRegulations.sectionTitle: Telehealth Regulations Across Our Licensed States
paragraphs: TeleDirectMD operates only where its physicians hold active licensure, currently 41 states plus Washington, DC. Each state sets its own telemedicine standards, and in every state a parent or legal guardian must consent to a minor's care. TeleDirectMD verifies that the child is physically located in a licensed state at the time of the visit; care is not provided to children outside the licensed footprint.

Some states require the prescribing physician to document permethrin resistance before prescribing second-line lice agents via telehealth. State-specific pages cite the controlling state statute. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

whatIsCondition.sectionTitle: What Is Head Lice in Children?
paragraphs: Head lice (Pediculus humanus capitis) are tiny wingless insects that live on the scalp and feed on blood. They spread mainly through head-to-head contact and are very common in school-age children. Lice cannot jump or fly and do not live long off the scalp.

Head lice are a nuisance, not a disease. Per the CDC clinical care guidance and the American Academy of Pediatrics 2015 head lice clinical report, lice do not transmit illness and are not a sign of poor hygiene. The main complication to watch for is a secondary skin infection from scratching.

TeleDirectMD focuses on uncomplicated head lice in children ages 5 to 17 that can be confirmed by video exam, with a parent present, and refers eyelash involvement or signs of secondary infection to in-person care.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric head lice in children ages 5 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Direct head-to-head contact:
items.text: the most common route of transmission, especially among children who play closely together.

items.label: Sharing personal items:
items.text: less commonly, sharing hats, combs, brushes, or pillows can spread lice.

items.label: School-age setting:
items.text: head lice are common among school-age children, including TeleDirectMD's 5 to 17 age range.

items.label: Biology of lice:
items.text: lice cannot jump or fly and do not survive long away from the scalp, so household spread is mostly through close contact.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every itchy scalp is head lice. Dandruff or seborrhea, hair casts or product residue, and scalp eczema or psoriasis can mimic lice. TeleDirectMD uses history and video exam to confirm live lice or viable nits before recommending treatment and directs atypical presentations to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Head Lice vs Dandruff
compareCards.text: Head lice are diagnosed by finding live lice or viable nits glued within a quarter inch of the scalp, especially behind the ears and at the nape. Dandruff and seborrhea produce flakes that brush off easily, whereas nits are firmly attached to hair shafts and do not slide off. This firm attachment is one of the most reliable distinguishing features.

compareCards.title: Nits vs Hair Casts and Product Residue
compareCards.text: Hair casts and product residue slide freely along the hair shaft, unlike true nits, which are cemented in place. Scalp eczema or psoriasis causes scaly, itchy patches without lice or nits. Secondary impetigo can develop from scratching and shows honey-colored crusting that may need antibiotics.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If live lice or viable nits cannot be confirmed by video, or there are signs of a secondary infection or eyelash involvement, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person care.

treatmentOptions.intro: First-line treatment is over-the-counter permethrin 1 percent, applied to damp hair and repeated about 9 days later. For documented resistance or treatment failure, a TeleDirectMD physician may prescribe spinosad, ivermectin lotion, or benzyl alcohol. School re-entry guidance is provided, and TeleDirectMD never prescribes oral lice treatments by telehealth without appropriate evaluation.

sections.title: First-line treatment
sections.text: Over-the-counter permethrin 1 percent (Nix) is applied to damp hair and repeated about 9 days later. The American Academy of Pediatrics 2015 clinical report and CDC identify it as a safe, effective first-line agent labeled from age 2 months, well below the age 5 floor.

sections.title: Resistant or treatment-failure cases
sections.text: For documented permethrin resistance or treatment failure, prescription options include spinosad 0.9 percent (Natroba), ivermectin lotion 0.5 percent (Sklice), and benzyl alcohol 5 percent (Ulesfia), each FDA-labeled from age 6 months. Persistent live lice after correct treatment usually indicates resistance rather than reinfestation.

sections.title: Home environment measures
sections.text: Wash recently used bedding and clothing in hot water, seal non-washable items for two weeks, and wet-comb with a nit comb every 2 to 3 days. Treat only household members who have live lice or viable nits, not everyone, and do not fumigate the home.

sections.title: School re-entry
sections.text: Per CDC and AAP, no-nit exclusion policies are not recommended, and children may return to school after the first treatment. TeleDirectMD provides return guidance and reassurance that lice are a nuisance, not a disease.

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Apply the chosen product exactly per label and repeat the second treatment on schedule, usually day 9.
Wet-comb with a fine-tooth nit comb every 2 to 3 days to remove nits.
Wash recently used bedding and clothing in hot water; seal non-washable items in a bag for 2 weeks.
Check household members and treat only those with live lice or viable nits.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: If itching or live lice persist after correct treatment, this suggests resistance and a second-line agent may be needed.
If sores from scratching develop honey-colored crusting, watch for secondary impetigo.
If spreading redness, pus, fever, or swollen neck glands develop, seek in-person care.
Follow up by video if the infestation is not clearing as expected.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Avoid head-to-head contact and do not share hats, combs, or brushes during an active infestation.
Per CDC and AAP, children may return to school after the first treatment; no-nit policies are not recommended.
Continue wet-combing to confirm the infestation has cleared.
Do not fumigate the home; focus on the scalp treatment and laundering recently used items.
Follow up if live lice persist after a correctly applied second treatment.

items.question: What is the first-line treatment TeleDirectMD recommends for head lice?
items.answer: Over-the-counter permethrin 1% (Nix) is first-line. TeleDirectMD recommends permethrin 1% for children ages 5 to 17, applied to damp hair and repeated about 9 days later, because the American Academy of Pediatrics 2015 clinical report and CDC identify it as a safe, effective first-line agent labeled from age 2 months. Prescription options are reserved for documented resistance or treatment failure.

items.question: Can my child go to school with head lice?
items.answer: Yes, after treatment begins. Per the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics 2015 head lice report, no-nit exclusion policies are not recommended, and children ages 5 to 17 may return to school after the first treatment. TeleDirectMD provides return guidance and counsels parents that head lice are a nuisance, not a disease, and do not reflect poor hygiene.

items.question: What does TeleDirectMD prescribe if over-the-counter lice treatment fails?
items.answer: For documented permethrin resistance or treatment failure in children ages 5 to 17, TeleDirectMD physicians can prescribe spinosad 0.9% (Natroba, ages 6 months and older), ivermectin lotion 0.5% (Sklice, ages 6 months and older), or benzyl alcohol 5% (Ulesfia, ages 6 months and older). These are reserved for second-line use. Persistent live lice after correct treatment usually indicates resistance rather than reinfestation.

items.question: How do I know if it's really lice and not dandruff?
items.answer: Lice are diagnosed by finding live lice or viable nits glued within a quarter inch of the scalp, especially behind the ears and at the nape. Unlike dandruff, which brushes off easily, nits are firmly attached to hair shafts. A TeleDirectMD physician confirms the diagnosis by video exam for children ages 5 to 17 before recommending treatment.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for a head lice visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any child ages 5 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD for head lice. The guardian's identity is verified, and the child must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the video visit.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD treat head lice in children under 5?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD treats head lice only for children ages 5 to 17. While permethrin is FDA-labeled from 2 months of age, TeleDirectMD's pediatric platform begins at age 5 for head lice and most non-conjunctivitis conditions. Families with younger children should consult their pediatrician, who can confirm the diagnosis and recommend an age-appropriate product in person.

items.question: Do I need to treat the whole house if my child has lice?
items.answer: Not the whole house. Per CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics, treat only household members who have live lice or viable nits, not everyone. TeleDirectMD counsels parents of children ages 5 to 17 to wash recently used bedding and clothing in hot water, seal non-washable items for two weeks, and wet-comb with a nit comb, rather than fumigating the home.

items.question: Can head lice spread disease?
items.answer: No. Head lice do not transmit any disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics 2015 clinical report describes head lice as a nuisance, not a health hazard, and not a sign of poor hygiene. TeleDirectMD treats children ages 5 to 17 mainly to relieve itching and stop spread; the main complication to watch for is a secondary skin infection from scratching.
